For Halloween, Pringles Takes Its Iconic Can To The Grave

  • 0shares
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:04
Instaread

Pringles has found perhaps the ultimate use for its famous can: spending eternity inside one.

For Halloween, the brand has launched Once You Drop, giving one fan the chance to win a real Pringles-shaped funeral urn alongside what it calls an “afterlifetime” supply of crisps: enough for roughly 200 years. To enter, U.S. fans sign a tongue-in-cheek “will and taste-ament” pledging their undying loyalty to the brand.

The Joke Comes From Real Brand History

As absurd as the idea sounds, Pringles did not invent the story for Halloween.

Fredric J. Baur, who designed the cylindrical Pringles can in the 1960s, was reportedly so proud of his creation that he asked for part of his ashes to be buried inside one. When he died in 2008, his family honored the request using an Original Pringles can.

Pringles has now turned that piece of brand lore into a physical product. The winner receives a personalized metal urn shaped like the familiar tube, complete with a removable lid and engraving. The campaign was created with BBDO New York and Weber Shandwick.

Commit To The Bit

The launch film stars TikTok creator Dan the Funeral Man, who is also an actual funeral director, inspecting a coffin and delivering the campaign with appropriately straight-faced professionalism. Entries remain open through October 22, with the winner expected to be notified around Halloween.

It works because Pringles commits completely to an idea that could easily have remained a throwaway social joke.

There is a real urn. A fake testament. A funeral director. Two centuries of crisps. Even the campaign title pushes the brand’s “Once You Pop, the Pop Don’t Stop” platform into the afterlife.

And underneath all the dark humor is an incredibly strong brand asset.

The Pringles tube is so recognizable that it can become an urn and still require almost no explanation. The packaging is the product, the joke and the advertising at the same time.

Most Halloween campaigns borrow something spooky for a few weeks.

Pringles looked into its own history and found something much stranger.

The Independent’s Social Commerce Shift Shows Why Publishers Are Rebuilding Around Audiences

The Independent’s social-commerce revenue narrowly overtook its SEO-based commerce revenue in September. That may sound like a small accounting milestone. It is actually a sharp signal of how publishers are trying to survive after the search-led growth model stopped looking dependable.

Independent Media CEO Christian Broughton described the gap as narrow and did not disclose the underlying figures. The point is therefore directional, not proof that social commerce has suddenly become a dominant business. But it shows where the company believes audience value is moving.

Advertisement

Social is becoming a revenue relationship

For years, publishers treated search and social as distribution channels. Search delivered intent. Social delivered reach. The website captured the audience, and advertising did much of the monetization. That arrangement now looks increasingly fragile as Google changes how discovery works, platforms retain more attention, and publishers compete with AI-generated answers for the click.

Broughton’s argument, as reported by Digiday, is that the answer is not simply to replace search traffic with more social traffic. Independent Media is building around four areas: AI, creator-led studio work, e-commerce, and membership. Together, those businesses are expected to represent nearly half of revenue in 2026 and grow by close to 30% year over year.

That is a different model from chasing the largest possible audience and hoping the advertising market follows. It puts more emphasis on trusted brands, repeat relationships, and products that can travel across platforms without becoming completely dependent on any one platform’s algorithm.

The company’s official Bulletin app makes the strategy visible at product level. It offers concise, swipeable updates, personalised topics and writers, notifications, audio, and puzzles. The product is not just another place to republish articles. It is an attempt to create a direct habit around the Independent brand.

AI only matters when it changes the economics

The same logic shapes the company’s AI work. The Independent has described Bulletin as an AI-enabled product with human editorial supervision, while Broughton told Digiday that AI tools are being used to apply style guidance, surface archive reporting, monitor organisations, and support a new live news team.

He claimed editors using those tools were six times as economically productive as colleagues in comparable roles who were not using them. That figure needs to be treated as an executive claim rather than an independently verified benchmark. Still, the operating principle is clear: AI is being judged against capacity and revenue, not novelty.

The Independent also says its conversational AI feature Eva reduced bounce rate by 10% and increased user journeys by 20%, although the company did not disclose the baselines. Again, the numbers are difficult to assess from the outside. The more important signal is that the publisher is trying to make AI useful at two points in the business: reducing repetitive newsroom work and helping audiences move deeper into its journalism.

That distinction matters for publishers and platforms alike. AI does not repair a weak business model simply because it can produce more content or summarise more quickly. It becomes strategically useful when it creates room for original reporting, podcasts, newsletters, documentaries, membership, or commerce products that audiences have a reason to return to.

The Independent’s social-commerce milestone is therefore less about social beating search than about the end of channel logic. Publishers can no longer assume that traffic source and business model will remain aligned. The stronger position belongs to the organisations that use platforms for discovery, then build enough trust and product depth to turn that attention into a relationship they can keep.
